title: Lincoln Loses His Son Willie
text:
William Wallace Lincoln, called Willie, was the third son of Abraham and Mary Lincoln. Bright, gentle and lively, he was ten when the family moved into the White House in 1861, and he and his younger brother Tad ran wild through its corridors.

In early February 1862, Willie fell ill with a fever, probably typhoid from the contaminated water supply. While he lay sick, the Lincolns held a large evening reception, and his parents kept slipping upstairs to see him. Tad fell ill too. Willie grew steadily worse and died on 20 February 1862.

Elizabeth Keckley, Mary Lincoln's dressmaker and friend, who was present, later recorded the president's grief as he looked at the boy's face. Lincoln said that his poor boy had been too good for this earth, that God had called him home, and that it was hard, hard to have him die. Keckley wrote that she had never seen a man so bowed down by grief.

All this happened in the middle of the Civil War, while Lincoln was directing the Union's armies. He went back to his work. Mary was overwhelmed and stopped appearing in public for months; she never again entered the room where Willie died. When Lincoln was assassinated three years later, Willie's coffin was placed on the funeral train beside his father's, and they were buried together in Springfield, Illinois.
lesson: Leaders carry private grief alongside public duty, and so do ordinary people at work. Remember that others may be bearing losses we cannot see.
people: Abraham Lincoln, Mary Todd Lincoln, Willie Lincoln, Tad Lincoln, Elizabeth Keckley
location: The White House, Washington, D.C., USA
source: Elizabeth Keckley, Behind the Scenes (1868), chapter 7; Michael Burlingame, Abraham Lincoln: A Life (2008)
